title: Equivalent Expressions, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with equivalent expressions, and then use Desmos as an equivalence checker and as a factor finder.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. Squaring x plus six does not mean squaring each term. Students write x squared plus thirty-six, and miss the middle term completely.
Squaring means multiplying the binomial by itself. The middle term is two times x times six, which is twelve x.
Trap two. Distributing a negative number across a subtraction flips the sign of every term. Students often keep the second sign the same.
Negative three times negative five is positive fifteen. So the correct result is negative three x plus fifteen.
Trap three. When you multiply powers with the same base, you add the exponents. Students multiply them, because the other rule, for a power of a power, is also on their mind.
Two plus three is five. So x squared times x cubed is x to the fifth. You multiply exponents only for a power of a power.

scenes.title: Trap 4: the coefficient in a power

beats.say: Trap four. When a whole term is raised to a power, the coefficient is raised too. Students apply the power only to the variable part.
Two cubed is eight, and five times three is fifteen. So the correct result is eight x to the fifteenth.

Trap five. In a fraction, you may cancel common factors, but never individual terms. A student might cancel x squared from the top and bottom of x squared minus sixteen over x squared plus seven x plus twelve.
beats.wrong_why: x^2 is a term, not a factor

beats.say: Factor first. The top is x minus four times x plus four, and the bottom is x plus three times x plus four. Now x plus four is a common factor, and it can cancel.
Desmos is a reliable equivalence checker. Graph the original expression, then graph each answer choice. The equivalent choice draws exactly on top of the original.

card.text: Equivalent graphs lie on top of each other

beats.say: Our example is two x minus three, times four x plus one, minus five x. We compare it with two choices, eight x squared minus fifteen x minus three, and eight x squared minus ten x minus three.
Open a fresh graph. We will type the original expression first, and then each choice.
Type y equals two x minus three, times four x plus one, minus five x. Desmos draws a parabola.
Now type the first choice, y equals eight x squared minus fifteen x minus three. Remember the right arrow after the exponent.
Now type the second choice, y equals eight x squared minus ten x minus three.
Only two curves are visible. The first choice lies exactly on top of the original, so they are equivalent. The second choice is a different curve, so it is wrong.
Desmos can also find factors. If the graph of a polynomial crosses the x axis at x equals four thirds, then three x minus four is a factor. Let us try three x squared minus x minus four.

card.sub: Find the factors from the intercepts

beats.say: We graph the polynomial and click its x-intercepts. Each intercept tells us one factor.
Type y equals three x squared minus x minus four. Desmos draws an upward-opening parabola.
Click the left intercept. It is at negative one, which means x plus one is a factor.
Click the right intercept. It is at one and one third, which means three x minus four is a factor. So the polynomial factors as three x minus four, times x plus one.
Now a practice problem. Write x plus five, times x minus two, plus three x, as a quadratic in standard form. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
First expand the product. We multiply each term of the first factor by each term of the second factor.
x times x is x squared. x times negative two is negative two x. Five times x is five x. Five times negative two is negative ten.
Combine the x terms. Negative two x plus five x plus three x is six x. So the standard form is x squared plus six x minus ten.
Check with x equal to two. The original is seven times zero, plus six, which is six. The answer is four plus twelve minus ten, which is also six.
To recap. Square a binomial by multiplying it by itself, add exponents when multiplying powers, and raise the coefficient too.
Distribute negatives to every term, and cancel only common factors, never single terms.
Use Desmos graphs to check equivalence, and intercepts to find factors. In the next topic, we study nonlinear equations and systems.
